meta.title: Symbiosis Unfold dataset
meta.notes: Curated, citation-backed relationships. Citations marked needed=true are intentionally left open rather than invented. dependence.{source,target} = how much that side depends on THIS particular partner (obligate | facultative | none); a parasite that needs some host but not this one is facultative. Drives the cascade and path-finder tools.

audit.summary: All non-needed citations checked against web records; all matched first author, year and venue. e51 not retrieved directly. e01 and e11 filled with almond-specific sources; e27 gained the biotin source (Nikoh 2014).

nodes.name: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi
nodes.fact: Fossil arbuscules in the ~400-million-year-old Rhynie chert show this partnership is about as old as land plants themselves.

nodes.name: Ectomycorrhizal fungi
nodes.fact: Mapped forest networks have shown single Douglas firs linked through ectomycorrhizal fungi to dozens of neighbouring trees.

nodes.name: Orchid mycorrhizal fungi
nodes.fact: Orchid seeds are dust-like with almost no food reserve; most cannot germinate in nature without one of these fungi feeding them.

nodes.name: Epichloë endophyte
nodes.fact: Lives entirely inside the grass and passes to the next generation through the seed—it never needs to leave its host.

nodes.name: Lichen fungus (horsehair lichen)
nodes.fact: Bryoria fremontii (black tree lichen) was pit-cooked and eaten by several Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest.

nodes.name: Cyphobasidium lichen yeast
nodes.fact: Its 2016 discovery in lichen cortices challenged the ~150-year-old 'one fungus + one alga' definition of a lichen.
nodes.tags_note: Lichen-yeast distribution poorly mapped; host Bryoria is boreal/temperate

nodes.name: Leafcutter ant fungus
nodes.fact: Produces swollen hyphal tips called gongylidia that appear to exist only to feed the ants.

nodes.name: Escovopsis
nodes.fact: A specialised mycoparasite known only from the gardens of fungus-growing ants.

nodes.name: Termitomyces
nodes.fact: Termitomyces mushrooms that sprout from termite mounds are prized wild edibles across Africa and Asia.

nodes.name: Laurel wilt fungus
nodes.fact: Since detection in Georgia in 2002, laurel wilt has killed a large share of redbay trees across the US Southeast.

nodes.name: Zombie-ant fungus
nodes.fact: Infected ants clamp onto a leaf vein in a 'death grip' at a height and humidity that suits the fungus's spore release.

nodes.name: Amphibian chytrid fungus
nodes.fact: Scheele et al. (2019) linked chytridiomycosis to declines in at least 501 amphibian species, including 90 presumed extinctions.

nodes.name: Brewer's/baker's yeast
nodes.fact: Industrial beer yeasts trace to a few domesticated lineages—a genuine case of humans domesticating a microbe.

nodes.name: Soybean rhizobia
nodes.fact: Nitrogenase is so oxygen-sensitive that the plant makes leghemoglobin to buffer it—why active nodules are pink inside.

nodes.name: Azolla cyanobiont
nodes.fact: Passed between fern generations and so degraded in its genome that it appears unable to live on its own.

nodes.name: Crown gall bacterium
nodes.fact: Its natural ability to insert DNA into plant genomes became the workhorse tool of plant genetic engineering.

nodes.name: Pseudonocardia
nodes.fact: On some fungus-growing ants it grows in specialised cuticle crypts—a living antibiotic dispenser on the ant's body.

nodes.name: Buchnera
nodes.fact: Its genome is ~640 kb—roughly one-seventh of E. coli's—after shedding genes it no longer needs inside aphid cells.

nodes.name: Hamiltonella
nodes.fact: Much of its anti-wasp protection comes from toxin genes carried by a bacteriophage (APSE) living inside the bacterium.

nodes.name: Wigglesworthia
nodes.fact: Supplies B vitamins missing from an all-blood diet; tsetse females cleared of it become sterile.

nodes.name: Wolbachia
nodes.fact: Estimated to infect roughly 40–65% of insect species—possibly the most widespread bacterial infection on Earth.

nodes.name: Bee core gut bacteria
nodes.fact: A small, consistent set of bacterial species makes up most of the honeybee gut community worldwide.

nodes.name: Rumen bacteria
nodes.fact: The microbes, not the cow, break down cellulose; the cow lives largely on their fermentation products.

nodes.name: Vibrio fischeri
nodes.fact: Each dawn the squid vents most of its bacteria into the sea and regrows the population by nightfall.
nodes.tags_note: Squid light organ crypt has no exact vocab match; animal-surface chosen as epithelial-lined

nodes.name: Endoriftia
nodes.fact: Oxidises hydrogen sulphide from vent fluid to fix carbon—photosynthesis-free primary production.
nodes.tags_note: Hosts live at Pacific vents, not strictly tropical; vocab has no Pacific/deep-ocean region

nodes.name: Lyme disease spirochete
nodes.fact: Lyme disease is named after Lyme, Connecticut, where a cluster of cases was investigated in the 1970s.

nodes.name: Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron
nodes.fact: Carries a huge repertoire of genes for breaking down plant polysaccharides that human enzymes can't touch.

nodes.name: Bifidobacterium infantis
nodes.fact: Human milk contains oligosaccharides the infant can't digest—they largely feed bacteria like this one.

nodes.name: Helicobacter pylori
nodes.fact: Barry Marshall drank a culture of it to help prove it causes gastritis; he and Robin Warren won the 2005 Nobel Prize.

nodes.name: Staphylococcus epidermidis
nodes.fact: One of the most common bacteria on human skin—and a leading cause of infections on implanted medical devices.

nodes.name: Almond
nodes.fact: Most commercial varieties are self-incompatible, so California orchards rent well over a million honeybee hives each bloom.

nodes.name: Soybean
nodes.fact: A top global protein crop, partly because its root nodules supply much of its own nitrogen.

nodes.name: Douglas fir
nodes.fact: Can live for more than 500 years and grow among the tallest trees on Earth.

nodes.name: Paper birch
nodes.fact: Its white bark is rich in betulin and was used for canoes and containers.

nodes.name: Ghost pipe
nodes.fact: Has no chlorophyll; it takes all its carbon from fungi, which take it from trees.

nodes.name: Terrestrial orchids
nodes.fact: Orchidaceae is one of the largest families of flowering plants, with roughly 28,000 species.

nodes.name: Azolla (mosquito fern)
nodes.fact: Used for centuries as a green manure in rice paddies in China and Vietnam.

nodes.name: Tall fescue
nodes.fact: Endophyte-infected pastures cause 'fescue toxicosis' in cattle, costing US producers hundreds of millions of dollars a year.

nodes.name: Avocado & redbay
nodes.fact: Avocado shares the laurel family with redbay, which is why laurel wilt threatens Florida's avocado groves.

nodes.name: Yucca
nodes.fact: Relies on a single moth lineage for pollination—no bees, no wind.

nodes.name: Figs
nodes.fact: There are 750+ fig species; the old 'one fig, one wasp' rule has many exceptions.

nodes.name: Heliconia
nodes.fact: Its curved flowers match the curved bills of the hummingbirds that pollinate it.

nodes.name: Whitebark pine
nodes.fact: Its cones don't open on their own; it depends almost entirely on Clark's nutcrackers to plant its seeds.

nodes.name: Bullhorn acacia
nodes.fact: Grows hollow thorns to house ants and feeds them nectar and protein-rich 'Beltian bodies'.

nodes.name: Early spider orchid
nodes.fact: Mimics the sex pheromone of female mining bees so precisely that males try to mate with the flower.

nodes.name: Maize
nodes.fact: Domesticated from teosinte in southern Mexico ~9,000 years ago; its husked cobs can't disperse seed without people.

nodes.name: Trebouxia (lichen alga)
nodes.fact: One of the most common green-algal partners in lichens worldwide.

nodes.name: Coral symbiotic algae
nodes.fact: These dinoflagellates can supply most of a reef coral's energy through photosynthesis.

nodes.name: Termite gut flagellates
nodes.fact: Lower termites can't digest wood without the flagellates packed into their hindgut.

nodes.name: Malaria parasite
nodes.fact: Malaria still kills hundreds of thousands of people a year, most of them young children in Africa.

nodes.name: Leafcutter ants
nodes.fact: They don't eat the leaves they cut—they feed them to a fungus they farm underground.

nodes.name: Fungus-growing termites
nodes.fact: Their mounds act as ventilation systems that help keep the fungus garden's climate stable.

nodes.name: Subterranean termites
nodes.fact: Among the most economically damaging structural pests in North America and Europe.

nodes.name: Redbay ambrosia beetle
nodes.fact: Females carry fungal spores in special pouches called mycangia.

nodes.name: Carpenter ants
nodes.fact: They nest in wood but don't eat it—unlike termites, they only excavate.

nodes.name: Aphids
nodes.fact: Many aphids reproduce clonally, born already carrying their own developing daughters ('telescoping generations').

nodes.name: Aphid parasitoid wasp
nodes.fact: Lays an egg inside a living aphid; the larva eats it from within, leaving a swollen 'mummy'.

nodes.name: Black garden ant
nodes.fact: Strokes aphids with its antennae to solicit droplets of honeydew—'milking' them.

nodes.name: Tsetse fly
nodes.fact: Gives birth to one fully grown larva at a time, fed on 'milk' secreted inside the mother.

nodes.name: Bed bug
nodes.fact: Feeds only on blood, a diet poor in B vitamins—hence its reliance on Wolbachia.

nodes.name: Fruit fly (D. simulans)
nodes.fact: Researchers watched Wolbachia spread through California populations of this fly in near real time.

nodes.name: Yellow fever mosquito
nodes.fact: Spread worldwide with human shipping; it breeds in tiny containers of water around homes.

nodes.name: Malaria mosquito
nodes.fact: Only females bite; they need the protein in blood to produce eggs.

nodes.name: Head louse
nodes.fact: Louse genetics have been used to estimate when humans started wearing clothing.

nodes.name: Yucca moth
nodes.fact: Females use specialised mouthpart tentacles to pack pollen onto the yucca stigma—deliberate pollination.

nodes.name: Fig wasps
nodes.fact: Wingless males spend their whole lives inside the fig, mating and chewing exit tunnels for the females.

nodes.name: Western honeybee
nodes.fact: Foragers share the direction and distance of food with the waggle dance.

nodes.name: Mining bees
nodes.fact: Solitary bees that nest in burrows dug into the ground.

nodes.name: Acacia ant
nodes.fact: Workers attack herbivores and prune away plants that grow too close to their host acacia.

nodes.name: Red-billed oxpecker
nodes.fact: Its Swahili name translates roughly as 'the rhino's guard'—its alarm calls warn rhinos of approaching people.

nodes.name: Cattle egret
nodes.fact: Colonised the Americas from Africa on its own in the late 1800s and spread alongside cattle ranching.

nodes.name: Common cuckoo
nodes.fact: Different female lineages lay eggs that mimic the eggs of their particular host species.

nodes.name: Reed warbler
nodes.fact: Rejects odd-looking eggs more often after seeing a cuckoo near its nest.

nodes.name: Great spotted cuckoo
nodes.fact: Unlike the common cuckoo, its chicks don't evict their host's eggs or nestlings.

nodes.name: Carrion crow
nodes.fact: Some carrion crow populations breed cooperatively, with helpers raising young that aren't their own.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.fact: In Yellowstone, ravens turn up at virtually every winter wolf kill.

nodes.name: Clark's nutcracker
nodes.fact: One bird can cache tens of thousands of pine seeds a season and relocate many of them months later.

nodes.name: Purple-throated carib
nodes.fact: Males and females have differently shaped bills, each matching a different Heliconia species.

nodes.name: Greater honeyguide
nodes.fact: Responds specifically to the Yao honey-hunters' 'brrr-hm' call, which makes guiding far more likely.

nodes.name: Varroa mite
nodes.fact: Jumped from the Asian honeybee to Apis mellifera in the 20th century and is now a leading driver of colony losses.

nodes.name: Bluestreak cleaner wrasse
nodes.fact: A single cleaner can inspect more than 2,000 client fish in a day.

nodes.name: Client reef fish
nodes.fact: Clients visit cleaning stations many times a day; removing cleaners can reduce local fish diversity.

nodes.name: Clownfish
nodes.fact: All clownfish start life male; the dominant fish in a group becomes the female.

nodes.name: Host sea anemone
nodes.fact: Its stinging cells don't fire on its resident clownfish, protected by the fish's mucus coat.

nodes.name: Reef-building corals
nodes.fact: Coral reefs cover well under 1% of the sea floor yet host roughly a quarter of known marine species.

nodes.name: Hawaiian bobtail squid
nodes.fact: Uses bacterial light to erase its own moonlit shadow from predators below (counter-illumination).
nodes.tags_note: Lives in shallow sandy Hawaiian flats; no benthic-sand vocab term, so intertidal/pelagic are approximations

nodes.name: Giant tubeworm
nodes.fact: Adults have no mouth or gut; a tissue packed with bacteria feeds them.
nodes.tags_note: Pacific vents, not strictly tropical; vocab has no deep-ocean region

nodes.name: Black rhinoceros
nodes.fact: Critically endangered; poaching for horn remains the main threat.

nodes.name: Cattle
nodes.fact: Rumen fermentation produces methane that cattle belch out—a significant greenhouse-gas source.

nodes.name: Grey wolf
nodes.fact: Reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in 1995.

nodes.name: Frogs & other amphibians
nodes.fact: Amphibians are the most threatened vertebrate class; roughly two in five species are at risk.

nodes.name: Blacklegged tick
nodes.fact: Larval ticks hatch uninfected and pick up Borrelia from their first blood meal.

nodes.name: White-footed mouse
nodes.fact: One of the most competent Lyme reservoirs: many larval ticks that feed on it become infected.

nodes.name: Domestic dog
nodes.fact: The first domesticated animal—domestication began well before agriculture.

nodes.name: Humans
nodes.fact: A typical person carries about as many bacterial cells as human cells (Sender et al. 2016).

edges.tldr: Fungal hyphae extend almond roots' reach for phosphorus and water in exchange for plant sugars. The fungus cannot complete its life cycle without a host.

gives.source: Phosphorus, zinc and water from soil beyond root reach

gets.target: Better nutrient uptake and drought tolerance

impact.ecological: Arbuscular mycorrhizae associate with most land plant species and shape soil structure.
impact.human: Managing mycorrhizae can reduce fertiliser needs in orchards; the size of the benefit varies by soil.

edges.confidence_note: The association in almond is documented: 62–73% root colonisation in California orchards (Vasilikiotis et al. 2020). The nutrient and drought benefit for almond specifically was not measured there.

edges.tldr: Usually a nutrient-for-sugar trade, but in phosphorus-rich soil or low light the plant can pay more carbon than it gets back. A textbook mutualism–parasitism continuum.

gets.target: Net benefit in low-P soils; net cost in high-P or shaded conditions

impact.ecological: Shows that 'mutualism' is a variable outcome, not a fixed label.
impact.human: Heavy phosphorus fertilisation can make the partnership worthless to crops.

edges.obligate: Fungi largely obligate; tree ecologically near-obligate in the wild
edges.tldr: Ectomycorrhizal fungi sheath Douglas fir root tips and trade soil nitrogen and phosphorus for sugars. Seedlings in the field rarely thrive without them.

gives.source: Nitrogen, phosphorus, water; some pathogen protection

gets.target: Nutrients from organic matter roots can't access

impact.ecological: Underpins conifer forest productivity and nutrient cycling.
impact.human: Forestry nurseries inoculate seedlings to improve outplanting success.

edges.tldr: Birch roots trade sugars for fungus-gathered nutrients, and the same fungal species can also colonise neighbouring conifers.

impact.ecological: Shared fungal partners physically connect different tree species.

edges.tldr: Labelled carbon has been measured moving between birch and fir through shared fungal networks. How much this matters, and the 'mother tree' story, are disputed.

gives.source: Small amounts of carbon (direction varies by season)

impact.ecological: If large, networks would change how we model forest competition; current evidence suggests effects are modest and context-specific.
impact.human: Widely popularised, and the popular version runs ahead of the evidence.

edges.confidence_note: Karst et al. 2023 argue field evidence for network-mediated benefits is weak and over-cited.

edges.tldr: A chlorophyll-free plant that taps into Russula fungi and takes carbon the fungi got from trees. It gives nothing back.

impact.ecological: Shows that fungal networks can be exploited by 'cheaters'.

edges.tldr: Orchid seedlings feed entirely on fungal carbon, so early on the orchid is effectively parasitic. Many green adults may pay some back, but evidence varies by species.

impact.ecological: Orchid distribution can be limited by where suitable fungi occur.
impact.human: Orchid conservation and propagation often requires the fungal partner.

citations.author: Rasmussen
citations.venue: Terrestrial Orchids: From Seed to Mycotrophic Plant (Cambridge UP)

edges.obligate: Neither (bacteria live free in soil; plants can use fertiliser N)
edges.tldr: Bacteria in root nodules convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia for the plant in exchange for carbon. Soybeans 'sanction' nodules that under-deliver.

impact.ecological: Biological nitrogen fixation is a major natural N input to ecosystems.
impact.human: Saves large amounts of synthetic nitrogen fertiliser in soybean farming.

edges.tldr: A nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium lives inside Azolla leaf cavities and passes to the next generation with the fern. Neither is found in nature without the other.

impact.ecological: Azolla blooms can rapidly add nitrogen to wetlands.
impact.human: Traditional green manure for rice paddies.

edges.tldr: A fungus inside the grass makes alkaloids that deter grazers and insects. Benefit to the grass depends on herbivore pressure and soil nutrients.

impact.ecological: Can shift pasture plant and insect communities.
impact.human: Causes fescue toxicosis in cattle; 'friendly' endophyte strains are sold commercially.

edges.tldr: The bacterium inserts some of its own DNA into plant cells and reprograms them into a tumour that produces food only it can use.

impact.ecological: A widespread soil pathogen.
impact.human: Crown gall harms nurseries and orchards, and the same mechanism powers plant biotechnology.

citations.author: Habbadi et al.
citations.venue: African and Mediterranean Agricultural Journal – Al Awamia

edges.confidence_note: Mechanism well established (Chilton 1977). The almond-specific record (tumorigenic isolates from Moroccan almond orchards) is in a regional journal and was confirmed from bibliographic listings only.

edges.tldr: The fungus builds a protective body and supplies water and minerals; the alga photosynthesises. Some researchers frame it as the fungus 'farming' the alga.

impact.ecological: Lichens colonise bare rock and bark, start soil formation and feed caribou in winter.
impact.human: Used as air-quality indicators.

edges.tldr: A basidiomycete yeast lives in the outer layer of many macrolichens, so some lichens are three-partner systems. Its role is not yet known.

impact.ecological: Changes how lichen symbiosis is defined.

edges.confidence_note: The yeast's presence is documented; the exchange and its benefit are not.

edges.tldr: Ants cut leaves to feed a fungus that they farm, weed and propagate; the fungus is their main food. Neither survives without the other.

gives.source: Cut leaves, weeding, dispersal to new nests

gets.target: Food, protection, transport to new colonies

impact.ecological: Leafcutters are dominant herbivores in the Neotropics and turn over large volumes of soil.
impact.human: Major agricultural pests in Latin America.

edges.tldr: A specialist fungus that attacks the ants' crop and can wipe out a garden.

impact.ecological: Drives the ants' hygiene behaviours and the antibiotic partnership.

edges.tldr: Bacteria on the ant cuticle make antibiotics that suppress Escovopsis. Prominent on Acromyrmex workers and largely absent from Atta workers.

impact.ecological: A three-way arms race: ant, crop, pathogen and defender.
impact.human: A source of novel antifungal compounds in drug discovery.

edges.confidence_note: How specific and how important the partnership is remains debated; it varies by ant genus.

edges.tldr: Termites cultivate Termitomyces on combs of chewed plant material; the fungus breaks down lignin and becomes the termites' food.

impact.ecological: Major decomposers in African and Asian savannas.
impact.human: Termitomyces mushrooms are valued food.

edges.obligate: Beetle obligate; fungus largely dependent on beetle for transport
edges.tldr: The beetle carries fungal spores in body pouches, plants them in tunnels in the wood, and feeds on the fungus.

gives.source: Transport and inoculation into new trees

impact.ecological: Invasive in the US Southeast.
impact.human: Spreads laurel wilt, which threatens avocado growing.

edges.tldr: The beetle's fungal crop is lethal to laurel-family trees, blocking their water transport.

impact.ecological: Has removed most mature redbays across much of their range.
impact.human: A threat to Florida's avocado industry.

edges.tldr: The fungus infects a worker ant, changes its behaviour so it bites a leaf vein, kills it, and sprouts a spore stalk from its head.

impact.ecological: May regulate ant populations; graveyards of infected ants form under colonies.

edges.tldr: Buchnera lives inside specialised aphid cells and makes essential amino acids missing from plant sap. The partnership is well over 150 million years old.

impact.ecological: Makes sap-feeding possible, one of the most successful insect lifestyles.
impact.human: Without Buchnera, aphids wouldn't be crop pests.

edges.tldr: A heritable bacterium that kills parasitoid-wasp larvae inside the aphid. Valuable when wasps are common; when they're scarce, infected aphids can lose out to uninfected ones.

impact.ecological: Changes how well biological pest control works.
impact.human: Can reduce the effectiveness of parasitoid releases against aphid pests.

edges.tldr: The wasp lays an egg inside an aphid and the larva consumes it from within.

impact.ecological: A natural regulator of aphid populations.
impact.human: Sold commercially for greenhouse biocontrol.

edges.tldr: Ants protect aphids from predators in exchange for sugary honeydew, but they also eat aphids when honeydew is less valuable than protein.

impact.ecological: Ant tending can boost aphid colonies and their damage to plants.
impact.human: Controlling ants is a known lever for aphid control.

citations.author: Stadler & Dixon
citations.venue: Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics

edges.tldr: Soybean aphids suck phloem sap, weakening plants and transmitting viruses.

impact.ecological: Invasive in North America since 2000.
impact.human: A major soybean pest that triggers widespread insecticide use.

edges.tldr: An intracellular bacterium supplies B vitamins that a blood-only diet lacks. Females without it can't reproduce.

impact.ecological: Makes blood-feeding possible for tsetse.
impact.human: Tsetse spread sleeping sickness; the symbiont is a potential control target.

edges.tldr: In bed bugs, Wolbachia lives in a dedicated organ and makes the B vitamin biotin. Here the usual reproductive parasite has become a nutritional partner.

impact.ecological: Shows a parasite turning into a mutualist.
impact.human: Bed bug control could target the symbiont.

edges.tldr: Wolbachia makes uninfected females' eggs fail when they mate with infected males (cytoplasmic incompatibility), so the infection spreads.

impact.ecological: Can drive rapid change through insect populations.
impact.human: The basis of Wolbachia-based mosquito control.

edges.tldr: The wMel Wolbachia strain was moved into Aedes aegypti, where it blocks dengue virus replication. Releases have cut dengue incidence.

gets.target: Slight fitness costs, reduced virus load

impact.ecological: A human-engineered symbiosis.
impact.human: Reduced dengue cases by 77% in a randomised trial in Yogyakarta.

edges.obligate: Females need blood meals to lay eggs
edges.tldr: A mosquito adapted to live alongside people; females feed on human blood and transmit dengue, Zika, chikungunya and yellow fever.

gives.target: Blood and water containers for breeding

gets.source: Protein for eggs and urban habitat

impact.ecological: Spread globally with trade.
impact.human: One of the most important disease vectors worldwide.

edges.tldr: A wingless insect that lives only on human scalps and feeds on blood several times a day.

impact.ecological: Co-evolved with humans over millions of years.
impact.human: Lice DNA helps date the origin of clothing.

edges.tldr: Female moths deliberately pollinate yucca flowers and lay eggs in them; the larvae eat some, but not all, of the seeds.

impact.ecological: A model of how 'cheating' is kept in check: plants abort overloaded flowers.

citations.author: Pellmyr
citations.venue: Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden

edges.tldr: Tiny wasps pollinate figs from inside the enclosed fig and raise their young in some of its flowers. Neither can reproduce without the other.

impact.ecological: Figs are keystone food for many tropical animals because they fruit year-round.
impact.human: Some commercial figs need wasp-pollination ('caprification').

citations.author: Janzen
citations.venue: Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics

edges.obligate: Almond near-obligate for yield (self-incompatible varieties); bee facultative
edges.tldr: Self-incompatible almond varieties need bees to move pollen between trees; bees get early-season pollen and nectar.

impact.ecological: Huge monocultures concentrate bee colonies and pathogens.
impact.human: California's almond crop depends on renting hives.

citations.author: Klein et al.
citations.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B

edges.obligate: Neither (managed populations depend heavily on beekeepers)
edges.tldr: People provide hives, medical care and transport; bees provide honey, wax and pollination services.

impact.ecological: Managed bees can compete with wild pollinators.
impact.human: Pollination is worth billions of dollars to agriculture each year.

citations.author: Crane
citations.venue: The World History of Beekeeping and Honey Hunting (Routledge)

edges.tldr: A mite that feeds mainly on bee fat-body tissue and spreads deformed wing virus.

gives.target: Food and brood cells to reproduce in

impact.ecological: Wild honeybee colonies have collapsed in many regions.
impact.human: A leading cause of beekeeper colony losses.

edges.tldr: A small, specialised set of gut bacteria digests pollen components and helps resist pathogens.

impact.ecological: A model system for gut microbiomes.
impact.human: Antibiotic use in hives can disrupt it.

edges.tldr: The orchid imitates a female bee's scent; males try to mate with the flower and carry pollen, getting nothing in return.

impact.ecological: A classic case of sexual deception.

edges.tldr: Hummingbird bills and Heliconia flowers match in curvature and length. Each sex of the bird mainly visits a different Heliconia.

impact.ecological: A clear case of coevolution between a bird and flowers.

edges.tldr: Nutcrackers cache thousands of pine seeds in the ground; the ones they don't retrieve sprout. The pine depends on this for dispersal.

impact.ecological: Whitebark pine is a keystone of high-elevation ecosystems.
impact.human: Whitebark pine is listed as threatened in the US.

edges.tldr: The tree houses and feeds the ants; the ants defend it from herbivores and competing plants.

impact.ecological: Unoccupied acacias are heavily damaged in experiments.

edges.tldr: Cleaners eat parasites off client fish, but sometimes cheat by biting nutritious mucus. Clients watch and choose honest cleaners.

impact.ecological: Removing cleaners lowers local fish diversity.

edges.tldr: The anemone's stinging tentacles shelter the clownfish; the fish chases off anemone predators and provides nutrients.

impact.ecological: Shared vulnerability to bleaching.
impact.human: Popular in the aquarium trade.

edges.tldr: The squid recruits glowing bacteria into a light organ, using the light to hide its shadow; the bacteria get food and a protected home.

impact.ecological: A model for how animals choose their microbes.
impact.human: Helped discover quorum sensing.

edges.tldr: Gutless tubeworms house chemosynthetic bacteria that use sulphide to produce food for the worm.

impact.ecological: Shows ecosystems can run on chemical energy instead of sunlight.

edges.tldr: Oxpeckers eat ticks but also keep wounds open to drink blood. Their alarm calls help rhinos detect approaching humans.

gives.source: Tick removal, alarm calls; but also wound feeding

impact.ecological: A cautionary tale about labelling relationships mutualistic.
impact.human: May help rhinos avoid poachers.

edges.tldr: Egrets follow grazing cattle and catch insects flushed by their hooves. The cattle appear unaffected.

impact.ecological: Helped the egret's spread across continents.

edges.tldr: Rumen microbes ferment cellulose into fatty acids the cow lives on; the cow provides a warm, steady fermentation chamber.

impact.ecological: Lets ruminants live on grass.
impact.human: Produces methane, a major greenhouse gas from agriculture.

citations.author: Hungate
citations.venue: The Rumen and Its Microbes (Academic Press)

edges.tldr: The cuckoo lays its egg in the warbler's nest; the hatchling evicts the host's eggs and is raised alone.

impact.ecological: A model coevolutionary arms race.

edges.tldr: One study found cuckoo chicks release a foul-smelling secretion that deters predators, so infested crow nests did better when predators were common. Later work disputed this.

gets.target: Net cost or net benefit, depending on predation

impact.ecological: Would be a rare example of a brood parasite becoming a mutualist.

edges.confidence_note: Contested: Soler et al. 2017 found no anti-predator effect in southern Spain, and Canestrari et al. published a formal reply. Whether the effect generalises is unresolved.

edges.tldr: Ravens follow wolves and scavenge their kills. They can take enough meat to be costly to small packs.

impact.ecological: Wolf kills subsidise many scavengers.

citations.author: Stahler, Heinrich & Smith
citations.note: widely cited for this finding; the record itself was not retrieved in the 2026-11 audit

edges.tldr: A skin fungus that disrupts amphibians' electrolyte balance, driving the largest recorded wildlife disease loss of biodiversity.

impact.ecological: Linked to declines in 500+ species and 90 presumed extinctions.
impact.human: A conservation crisis spread partly by the global wildlife trade.

edges.tldr: Larval and nymphal ticks feed on white-footed mice, which efficiently infect them with Lyme bacteria.

impact.ecological: Host community make-up shapes Lyme risk.
impact.human: Mouse density can predict Lyme risk.

edges.obligate: Borrelia obligate on the tick–host cycle
edges.tldr: The spirochete lives in the tick's gut and moves to its salivary glands during feeding. Effects on the tick are small and debated.

impact.ecological: The vector link in the Lyme cycle.
impact.human: The route by which Lyme disease reaches people.

edges.confidence_note: 'Commensalism' simplifies evidence on tick fitness effects, which is mixed.

edges.tldr: Spread by tick bites, causing Lyme disease. Humans don't pass it on, so the bacteria gain nothing.

impact.ecological: Humans are incidental to its cycle.
impact.human: The most common vector-borne disease in the US.

edges.tldr: A dominant gut bacterium breaks down dietary fibre into short-chain fatty acids we absorb, and shapes gut development.

gives.target: Short-chain fatty acids, gut maturation signals

impact.ecological: Part of a microbial community with as many cells as the body.
impact.human: Linked to metabolism and immune health.

edges.tldr: Breast milk contains sugars that infants can't digest but this bacterium can. It thrives on them and helps protect the infant gut.

impact.ecological: A diet that seems to have evolved to feed a microbe.
impact.human: Drives research on infant probiotics.

edges.tldr: A stomach bacterium that causes ulcers and gastric cancer in some carriers, but may lower risks of reflux and asthma.

impact.ecological: Has accompanied humans for at least ~60,000 years.
impact.human: Its removal is a public-health trade-off.

edges.tldr: Usually a harmless skin resident that crowds out pathogens, but a common cause of infections on implants and catheters.

impact.ecological: A key part of the skin microbiome.
impact.human: A leading cause of hospital device infections.

edges.tldr: Wild honeyguides lead honey-hunters to bee nests in response to specific calls; people open the nests and leave wax for the birds.

impact.ecological: A rare cooperation between free-living wild animals and people.
impact.human: A culturally important practice in parts of Africa.

edges.tldr: Wolves that associated with humans became dogs, gaining food and shelter while providing hunting help, guarding and companionship.

impact.ecological: Free-ranging dogs affect wildlife.
impact.human: The oldest domestic partnership.

edges.tldr: People turned teosinte into maize, whose cobs can't release their seeds. Maize now depends entirely on humans to reproduce.

impact.ecological: Maize covers huge areas of land.
impact.human: One of the world's top staple crops.

edges.tldr: People spread and selectively bred yeasts for bread, beer and wine; domesticated strains carry clear genetic signatures of this.

impact.human: The foundation of baking and brewing; a key lab model organism.

edges.obligate: Coral effectively obligate; algae also free-living
edges.tldr: Algae in coral tissue supply most of the coral's energy. Under heat stress the partnership breaks down and the coral expels them ('bleaching').

impact.ecological: The energy base of coral reefs.
impact.human: Recurrent mass bleaching threatens fisheries, tourism and coastal protection.

edges.tldr: Flagellate protists in the termite hindgut break down cellulose from wood. Termites cleared of them starve.

impact.ecological: Major contributors to wood decomposition.
impact.human: Termites damage buildings; their gut is studied for biofuel enzymes.

edges.tldr: The malaria parasite reproduces sexually inside Anopheles mosquitoes and reaches their salivary glands to be passed on.

gives.target: A host for sexual reproduction and transmission

impact.ecological: A key vector–parasite link.
impact.human: Ronald Ross's 1897 discovery transformed malaria control.

edges.tldr: The parasite multiplies in human liver and red blood cells, causing malaria.

impact.ecological: Has shaped human evolution, for example the sickle-cell trait.
impact.human: Hundreds of thousands of deaths per year.

edges.tldr: Female Anopheles feed on human blood, carrying Plasmodium between people.

impact.human: The only vectors of human malaria.

chains.name: Fungus-farming ants
chains.summary: Ants farm a fungus; a specialist parasite attacks the crop; antibiotic bacteria defend it.

chains.name: Aphid protection stack
chains.summary: A sap-feeder kept alive by one bacterium, defended by another, farmed by ants, hunted by wasps, and damaging nitrogen-fixing soybeans.

chains.name: Almond supply chain
chains.summary: Humans rent bees, bees pollinate almonds, almonds trade sugars with soil fungi; mites and gut bacteria shape bee health.

chains.name: Mycoheterotrophy
chains.summary: Trees feed fungi; a chlorophyll-free plant taps those fungi; birch shares the network.

chains.name: Laurel wilt
chains.summary: An invasive beetle's fungal crop kills redbay and avocado.

chains.name: Wolbachia vs dengue
chains.summary: A reproductive parasite turned public-health tool.

chains.name: Lyme disease cycle
chains.summary: Mice infect ticks, ticks carry Borrelia, people get sick.

chains.name: Three-partner lichen
chains.summary: Fungus + alga + a recently discovered yeast.

chains.name: Pasture
chains.summary: Egrets ride with cattle; cattle depend on rumen microbes to eat grass.

chains.name: The honey hunt
chains.summary: A wild bird guides people to bees' nests; humans also keep the same bees.

chains.name: Malaria
chains.summary: A protist parasite moves between mosquitoes and people.
